source.title: A Solvable Model of Neural Scaling Laws
source.authors: A. Maloney; Daniel A. Roberts; J. Sully

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives and simulates test-loss curves in a generalized linear random-feature model, a different method and model class from deep-network double-descent experiments. It also assesses how regularization changes the curve.
record.gate_note: The paper's own random-feature-model calculations and simulations report test loss as model size and training-set size vary. It discusses epoch-wise behavior but does not test it. Statements about double descent in cited papers are not treated as results here. Appendix A's simpler linear-model comparison changes task complexity with feature count, so it is not recorded as a direct test of the fixed-task size claim.
record.test_reason: The paper's own analysis gives a closed-form test loss (Eq. 163) for a solvable random-feature linear regression model, checked by simulations (Fig. 8). In the ridgeless limit the loss diverges at N=T, as a function of both model size and training-set size. With optimized ridge it is monotone (§4.2, Fig. 11). This is a new, non-deep-network setting with its own results on double descent, so it bears on V3, V4 and V6. It is not a deep network, so V1 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The paper's main conclusion concerns neural scaling laws: power-law data spectra extended by nonlinear features, the optimality of equiparameterization, and breakdown at latent size M. On double descent, the authors say the ridgeless model shows it, with a peak at N=T. They call it an artifact of not regularizing near N∼T: properly regularized loss decreases monotonically with size, so double descent is not relevant to the practical regime.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses an analytically tractable random-feature linear regression model and random-matrix calculations, with numerical simulations for verification. It does not reproduce deep-network size, epoch, or data sweeps from the original studies.
record.method_sensitivity: The curve changes with regularization: the unregularized model has a peak at equiparameterization, while optimized ridge regularization removes it. The paper also describes changes across noise and finite-latent-space regimes.

fits_no_version.finding: When both N and T exceed the latent dimension M, the label-noise contribution gives a universal ∼1/T test-loss falloff, with or without regularization. Without noise, the loss drops abruptly to zero as T reaches M.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling-law breakdown at the latent-space size: test loss changes power once resources exceed the data's latent dimension.

record.problems: Evidence is for a stylized generalized linear random-feature model, not deep networks. Results rely on large-dimension random-matrix approximations and simulations; uncertainty estimates are not reported. Epoch-wise behavior and the broad cross-model generalization are not tested.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-bearing results were omitted. The paper's cited double-descent findings are not its own results; its appendix's simpler linear-model comparison changes task complexity with feature count and is not treated as a direct fixed-task capacity test.

untested.parts: All of it: no deep networks are trained, and the model-size sweep is in a linear random-feature model.
All of it: the solution is analytic or converged, with no epoch-wise curve.
All of it: no effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations.
Triple or multiple descent. Separating the effect of label noise from feature variance on peak height is not done as a systematic test.
All of it: there is no recount of effective parameters. The authors' 'artifact' claim concerns the ridgeless limit, not complexity counting.
Model classes beyond this one random-feature linear model.

missing.what: The label-noise term of the test loss also diverges at N=T: σε²/2 × 1/(N/T−1) or 1/(T/N−1), Eq. 86. This shows label noise adds to the peak and breaks the T↔N symmetry. It is relevant to the noise part of V6.

Appendix A gives a plain linear model on isotropic (MP) data with a fixed-N sweep of T. The loss diverges at T=N only through label noise; the authors state it would be zero in the noiseless limit. This bears on V6 (noise drives the peak) and on V3 (more data hurts near T=N), and avoids the task-complexity confound the record cites, since N is fixed.
missing.locator: Appendix A.1, Eq. (227), Fig. 15 left; A.2, Eq. (230), Fig. 16

record.verdict_notes: I dropped V1 because the system is a linear random-feature regression, not a deep network. Tranche is T3 rather than T2: double descent is secondary to the paper's scaling-law aim, but its own solved model gives results on it. Peaks in this model arise even with zero label noise, from random-feature sampling noise; this fits V6's 'or variance' wording. Nakkiran et al. (arXiv:1912.02292) is cited as a reference, not as this study's own result, and this study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The model-size curve is tested in the paper's generalized linear random-feature model, not in deep networks or the original deep-network settings.
No test-loss sweep over training epochs or training time.
Tested in the random-feature model near the feature/sample equiparameterization point, not in the original deep-network settings.
The curve is examined in one generalized linear random-feature model; the claim across model classes is not established.
The paper does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and samples.

The model's unregularized peak and its removal under optimized ridge regularization are examined. The paper does not test triple or multiple descent, nor systematically isolate label-noise or variance causes across conditions.
No test of whether counting an effective number of parameters turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: joint generative data and random feature model (generalized linear regression)
rows.size_stated: N features; example simulations use M=6000 and α=1.0
rows.operation_detail: Sweep model feature count N at fixed training-set size in the ridgeless model.
rows.measure: Test loss as a function of model size
rows.value: For fixed T, test loss has a local minimum at N=N*, rises to a non-analytic peak at N=T, then improves asymptotically for N>T. The authors report the corresponding double-descent shape.
rows.note: The authors note that the first descent can include a local minimum before the peak. This is a random-feature regression model, not a deep network.
rows.check: The subject is a linear random-feature regression, not a deep network, so the row does not bear on V1, which names deep networks. For V4 the curve shows a first-descent local minimum, a peak at N=T and a further descent. For V6 the peak appears with zero label noise. The authors attribute it to noise in the random features (§3.2.3).

rows.subject: joint generative data and random feature model (generalized linear regression)
rows.size_stated: N features; Fig. 8 uses M=6000 and α=1.0
rows.operation_detail: Sweep model feature count N with the ridge parameter optimized.
rows.measure: Test loss as a function of model size
rows.value: With optimized ridge regularization, test loss decreases monotonically with model size and has no special behavior around N=T.
rows.note: The authors characterize the unregularized double-descent peak as an artifact of not regularizing around N≈T.
rows.check: The row's state should be read against V6, where the peak disappearing under optimal regularization is the predicted effect, so it is observed rather than absent. Remove V1 (not a deep network). Fig. 11 is a sketch whose regularized curves come from the phenomenological fit (172). The text says simulations back the comparison, but no simulated N-sweep under γ* is shown.

rows.subject: joint generative data and random feature model (generalized linear regression)
rows.size_stated: N features; Fig. 8 uses M=6000 and α=1.0
rows.operation_detail: Sweep training-set size T at fixed feature count.
rows.measure: Test loss as a function of training-set size
rows.value: By the reported T↔N symmetry of the noiseless ridgeless loss, the loss peaks at T=N; increasing T toward that point raises test loss.
rows.note: This supports more-data-can-hurt behavior near the sample/feature threshold in this model and condition.
rows.check: Direct evidence exists beyond the symmetry argument: Fig. 8 (top left, γ=0, σε=0) shows loss against T for fixed N, peaking at T=N. Add Fig. 8 top-left as the locator.

rows.operation_detail: Evaluate the test-loss contribution from independently added training-label noise across sample/model regimes.

conditions.value: ridgeless and optimized ridge cases are shown
N,T>M in the reported large-resource falloff

rows.value: For N,T>M, the authors report a universal ∼1/T falloff of test loss with label noise; the ridgeless contribution is given by Eq. (186), and an interpolating regularized fit by Eq. (188).
rows.note: This reports a noise-dependent loss regime, but does not isolate whether label noise causes the double-descent peak.
rows.check: This row concerns the ∼1/T label-noise falloff when N,T>M, a scaling-law breakdown regime. It does not measure the double-descent peak or whether noise drives it, so it bears on no version.

relationships.condition: Noiseless, ridgeless random-feature linear regression, N,T<M, fixed N
relationships.reason: The test loss rises as T approaches N and diverges at T=N, by the formula and simulations in Fig. 8 (r3).
relationships.display_finding: Theory and simulations showed test loss rising as T approached N and diverging at T = N.

relationships.condition: Ridgeless random-feature linear regression, fixed T, N,T<M
relationships.reason: Loss has a local minimum at N*, peaks at N=T, then decreases for N>T: a double-descent curve outside deep networks (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Loss reached a local minimum at N*, peaked at N=T, and decreased again for N>T.

relationships.condition: Random-feature linear regression, σε=0, ridgeless vs optimized ridge
relationships.reason: The peak at N=T appears without regularization, attributed to feature-sampling noise. It vanishes under optimal ridge, leaving monotone loss (r1, r2); the regularized curve is partly from a fitted formula.
relationships.display_finding: With σε = 0, unregularized loss peaked at N = T because of feature-sampling noise, while optimal ridge yielded monotone loss.
